short: A 23-ton French tank with a field gun, an electric drive, and tracks far too short.
full:
The Saint-Chamond came out of a rivalry rather than a plan: the artillery directorate ordered 400 on 8 April 1916 from a design by Colonel Émile Rimailho, in parallel with the Schneider and without much co-ordination between them. It was the better-armed machine, carrying a full 75 mm field gun in the bow and four machine guns for a crew of eight, and it was driven through a Crochat-Collardeau petrol-electric transmission that gave unusually fine control. But the armoured body overhung a short Holt track frame at both ends, so the tank grounded itself on anything but level going.

Sixteen went into action at the Laffaux mill on 5 May 1917; most bellied in the German trenches. The type served through 1917 and 1918 in ever more limited roles, its crews increasingly unwilling to take it into broken ground, and by the last offensives it was largely a supply and gun-tractor vehicle. Four hundred were built before production ended in July 1918, and almost all were scrapped soon after the war.
